rows: The two big front eyes see only a small patch, but they see it sharply. A typical jumping spider resolves about 3.8 cycles per degree there, and Portia reaches about 12.5, which is close to a bird.
A view all the way round
Three more pairs of small eyes are spaced around the head and together cover almost the whole circle. Their picture is soft, between 0.3 and 1.3 cycles per degree.
The front eyes carry an ultraviolet pigment near 370 nm and a green pigment near 530 nm. Colour is built from those two, so reds and greens run together and ultraviolet counts as a colour of its own.
Still things vanish at the sides
The side eyes behave as though completely blind to stationary objects. A light that only goes on and off draws no turn, and a target that moves does. They are also described as seeing without colour.

The retinas behind the front lenses sweep side to side across what they inspect with a period of 1 to 2 seconds. They also twist about 20 to 30 degrees each way, holding each extreme for several seconds.

The size and position of the sharp patch, the ring where the side eyes take over, the blue channel standing in for ultraviolet, the whole picture's sharpness drawn from a range, the grey sides and the drawing styles are the app's choices.

claims.how: R28 states the side eyes cover almost the entire 360 degrees around the animal.
The middle of 0.3 and 1.3 cycles per degree for the side eyes is 0.8.
A two pigment matrix built from the 370 nm ultraviolet peak (R55) and the 530 nm green peak (R54); the mapping is the app's.
R2 gives 3.8 cycles per degree for the principal eyes of Phidippus johnsoni.
Secondary eyes are described as monochromatic, so saturation is set to 0, which is the app's mapping.
Amplitude 2 degrees is the minimum in R134 and 1.5 seconds is the middle of the 1 to 2 second period in R129.
25 degrees is the middle of 20 to 30, 2000 ms is the stated 2 s to turn and 3500 ms is the middle of the 2 to 5 s hold.
